messages.author: c21e804e07c5e732
messages.subject: meaning of boxplot
parts:
Hi,

It seems that boxplot may slight differently depending on the plotting function.

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box_plot#Alternative_forms

I don't see the definition of boxplot on ggplot2 document page.

http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/geom_boxplot.html

I think in ggplot boxplot "the bottom and top of the box are always
the 25th and 75th percentile (the lower and upper quartiles,
respectively), and the band near the middle of the box", right? Could
anybody let me know what the meanings of the whiskers?

--
Regards,
Peng

messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Re: meaning of boxplot
parts:
http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box_plot

The definition of the whiskers of a box plot is given in that entry.

FYI, there are nine potential ways to define quantiles in R, following
Hyndman and Fan (1996). See ?quantile.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.subject: Re: meaning of boxplot
parts:
Hi Peng,

If you want to see how the calculations are performed, you are better
off looking at the documentation for the relevant "stat" than the
"geom". In this case, take a look at stat_boxplot here:
http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/stat_boxplot.html

That will also lead you to the relevant source code if you wanted to
see exactly how all of those were operationalized. For example, as
Dennis pointed out, which algorithm was used to calculate the
quantiles.

Hope this helps,

Josh

messages.author: daf017f67eba24e8
messages.subject: Re: meaning of boxplot
parts:
unfortunately, that's not *exactly* what it does. here's code I posted just the other day, in another thread, which performs the default calculation as in the source (taken from the source)

stats <- function(y, coef=1.5) { 
  qs <- c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1)
  stats <- as.numeric(quantile(y, qs))
  names(stats) <- c("ymin", "lower", "middle", "upper", "ymax")
  iqr <- diff(stats[c(2, 4)])     
  outliers <- y < (stats[2] - coef * iqr) | y > (stats[4] + coef * iqr)
  if (any(outliers)) stats[c(1, 5)] <- range(y[!outliers], na.rm=TRUE)  
  stats
}

so if there are any outliers beyond +-1.5*IQR then the ymin and ymax are set to the extremes of the non-outlier data.

I agree, it's annoying that the documentation isnt fully clear here. if you try to check what you get from geom_boxplot() against your own calculations based on the documentation, they dont match. So you have to read the source. 

If you dont read the source, then you can always use the keywords to geom_boxplot to make sure you're getting what you expect... why not just do that? That's what I did when I originally had this problem.

The documentation is one drawback of ggplot2, approaching it with "should" could drive one nuts. (Just a practical consideration). There is a tension in free and open-source software between providing good tools and providing their documentation. Developers like writing tools, not documenting them. At the same time, they want people to actually be able to use them... To help with that, R generally makes it really easy to read the source which, if written well, should be self-documenting. However navigating the ggplot2 proto code is even another barrier to reading the source in this case. Fortunately, there are nice people on this list who like helping. Documentation is nice, but there are also some perks of an email list.

best,

James

On Sat, Jun 25, 2011 at 22:14, James McCreight <mccr...@gmail.com> wrote:
unfortunately, that's not *exactly* what it does. here's code I posted just the other day, in another thread, which performs the default calculation as in the source (taken from the source)

stats <- function(y, coef=1.5) { 
  qs <- c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1)
  stats <- as.numeric(quantile(y, qs))
  names(stats) <- c("ymin", "lower", "middle", "upper", "ymax")
  iqr <- diff(stats[c(2, 4)])     
  outliers <- y < (stats[2] - coef * iqr) | y > (stats[4] + coef * iqr)
  if (any(outliers)) stats[c(1, 5)] <- range(y[!outliers], na.rm=TRUE)  
  stats
}

so if there are any outliers beyond +-1.5*IQR then the ymin and ymax are set to the extremes of the non-outlier data.

I agree, it's annoying that the documentation isnt fully clear here. if you try to check what you get from geom_boxplot() against your own calculations based on the documentation, they dont match. So you have to read the source. 

If you dont read the source, then you can always use the keywords to geom_boxplot to make sure you're getting what you expect... why not just do that? That's what I did when I originally had this problem.

The documentation is one drawback of ggplot2, approaching it with "should" could drive one nuts. (Just a practical consideration). If you're interested in helping document ggplot2, I'm slowly making it
easier and easier to get going. I recently release the devtools
package to cran. This means that you can easily install the version
of roxygen you need to produce the documentation:

install.packages("devtools")
library(devtools)
install_github("roxygen")

You then need to create a fork of the develop branch of ggplot2
(https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/tree/develop), clone it on your
local computer, and you then you can modify the documentation. In R

document("ggplot2")
dev_mode()
install("ggplot2")

will update the documentation, and reinstall so you can check your
changes. You then commit you changes and issue a pull request. This
takes a little bit of learning, but isn't too hard, and if you're
interested, I'm happy to get you up and running.

I have a student helping me out with documentation this summer. You
can see what he's been working on at:
https://github.com/JakeRuss/ggplot2/commits/develop

> Ggplot has interesting documentation because what's in the pdf and in the
> help files (e.g. ?stat_boxplot) is a mere shadow of what's on the web page.

The web page is built from exactly the same sources that generate the
R documentation, so there shouldn't be any differences. That said,
the website is a bit out of date, and that may account for a few
differences.

> Who uses the former?? I think it makes sense for the user community to have
> wiki version of the web documentation. Another possibility is having a repo
> on git hub for the html or having it in markdown. It would be a trememdous
> thing to be able to convert this into .Rd files. However, I'm not sure how
> that would interface with Roxygen documentation or if one would win out. I
> know almost nothing about Roxygen, other than these are ideas which might
> make it into Hadley's branch.

Github is making it easier and easier to make changes to source
online. If you have a (free) github account, on any source file
you'll see a link to "edit this file", which allows you to edit on the
website, and then automatically send me a request to include your
change (https://github.com/blog/844-forking-with-the-edit-button).
Again, if anyone was interested in writing up instructions on how to
do this, I'd be happy to help out.
